questions.statement: A research paper opens with a paragraph that states the problem, reviews the literature and ends with a research question. This paragraph is the:
questions.context: A reader identifies the standard sections of a research article in a social science journal.

options.text: introduction
options.feedback: Correct! The introduction frames the problem, situates the study and states the research question.

options.text: conclusion
options.feedback: The conclusion presents the findings, not the research question.

options.text: methodology
options.feedback: The methodology describes how the data were gathered.

options.text: appendix
options.feedback: An appendix holds supplementary material such as tables.

questions.explanation:
Academic texts follow a recognised structure, and the first paragraph that frames the problem and poses the question is the introduction.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In an academic article, a section that describes the sample, the instruments and the procedure is called:
questions.context: A reader looks for the part of a study that explains how the information was collected.

options.text: discussion
options.feedback: The discussion interprets the results.

options.text: method
options.feedback: Correct! The section that describes the sample, the instruments and the procedure is the method.

options.text: abstract
options.feedback: The abstract summarises the whole article in a few lines.

options.text: references
options.feedback: The references list the sources cited.

questions.explanation:
Naming the section depends on recognising its function. Description of the data collection is the method.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The phrase 'these findings are consistent with earlier work' in a paper most probably means:
questions.context: A researcher compares the results of a new study with those reported in earlier articles.

options.text: the results contradict the previous research.
options.feedback: A contradiction would be expressed with 'in contrast' or 'inconsistent with'.

options.text: the previous research was badly designed.
options.feedback: Nothing in the phrase criticises the design of the previous work.

options.text: the results agree with what previous research found.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Consistent with' is a standard formula meaning that the results agree with earlier research.

options.text: the results were copied from an older study.
options.feedback: Agreement with other studies is not the same as having copied them.

questions.explanation:
Academic hedging phrases carry a fixed meaning. 'Consistent with' signals agreement, not causation and not criticism.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase introduces a limitation of a study in an academic article?
questions.context: A reader identifies the part of a paper in which the author states the boundaries of the research.

options.text: The results were highly significant.
options.feedback: Significance strengthens a finding rather than limiting it.

options.text: The data support the hypothesis.
options.feedback: Supporting a hypothesis is a positive claim, not a limitation.

options.text: The method was replicated twice.
options.feedback: Replication strengthens a method rather than restricting it.

options.text: The sample was limited to one region.
options.feedback: Correct! Restricting the sample to one region is a boundary of the study, which is a limitation.

questions.explanation:
A limitation names a boundary of the design. The other three options strengthen the claims, which is what the limitations section does not do.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In a paper, the sentence 'We operationalised participation as weekly attendance' means the authors:
questions.context: A methods section explains how an abstract idea was turned into something that could be counted.

options.text: defined how the key concept was measured.
options.feedback: Correct! To operationalise is to define how a concept will be measured, here by weekly attendance.

options.text: rejected the usual definition of participation.
options.feedback: The sentence states a definition, not a rejection of one.

options.text: proved that attendance rose during the study.
options.feedback: The sentence describes the measurement, not a result about it.

options.text: asked participants to change their behaviour.
options.feedback: No instruction to the participants is given in that sentence.

questions.explanation:
'Operationalise' is a technical term. It names the step of converting a concept into a measurable indicator.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A citation such as (Ramirez, 2019) inside a running sentence usually indicates:
questions.context: A reader encounters an author and a year in brackets inside the sentences of a research article.

options.text: a quotation reproduced word for word.
options.feedback: A word-for-word quotation also carries a page number.

options.text: a source the author is referring to.
options.feedback: Correct! The name and the year identify the source being referred to at that point.

options.text: a footnote with a legal comment.
options.feedback: A footnote marker is a symbol, not a name and a year.

options.text: a list of the works cited at the end.
options.feedback: The list at the end of the article is the reference list, not the in-text citation.

questions.explanation:
An in-text citation points back to a source. Only a direct quotation and a paraphrase are marked with a page number as well.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which best describes the role of the discussion section of a research article?
questions.context: A student distinguishes the parts of a standard research article.

options.text: It reports the number of participants in the study.
options.feedback: The sample belongs to the method section.

options.text: It lists the sources consulted by the author.
options.feedback: The sources belong to the references.

options.text: It interprets the results and relates them to the literature.
options.feedback: Correct! The discussion interprets the findings and sets them against what was already known.

options.text: It states the question the study sets out to answer.
options.feedback: The research question belongs to the introduction.

questions.explanation:
Sections have distinct functions. The discussion explains what the results mean, which is neither the procedure nor the list of sources.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The word 'significant' in a sentence such as 'the difference was statistically significant' most probably means:
questions.context: A student reads a results section in which differences between groups are described as significant.

options.text: the difference was very large in size.
options.feedback: Significance says nothing about the size of the difference.

options.text: the difference was important to the author personally.
options.feedback: It is a technical measure, not a personal judgement.

options.text: the difference was measured in a biased way.
options.feedback: Bias is a problem with the design, not the definition of significance.

options.text: the difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone.
options.feedback: Correct! Statistical significance means the result is unlikely to have arisen by chance alone.

questions.explanation:
In academic writing 'significant' is a technical term about probability, not about size. The two senses are frequently confused.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which expression would you expect in the limitations of a study rather than in its abstract?
questions.context: A reader compares the content of the abstract of a study with the content of its limitations section.

options.text: The study did not include a control group.
options.feedback: Correct! The absence of a control group is a boundary of the design and belongs in the limitations.

options.text: The study examines how teenagers use social media.
options.feedback: The topic of the study appears in the abstract.

options.text: The study was carried out in two schools.
options.feedback: The setting of the study is a normal part of the method described in the abstract.

options.text: The findings suggest a link between the two variables.
options.feedback: The main finding is what the abstract reports.

questions.explanation:
The abstract presents the topic, the method and the main finding. A boundary of the design belongs to the limitations.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In an academic text, 'the data suggest' is weaker than 'the data prove' because:
questions.context: A student notices that a researcher chooses 'suggest' rather than 'prove' when presenting results.

options.text: saying 'prove' is not polite in academic writing.
options.feedback: The choice is about the strength of the claim, not about politeness.

options.text: observation always allows more than one explanation.
options.feedback: Correct! Data can be explained in more than one way, so a researcher states a suggestion rather than a proof.

options.text: the word 'data' is only used for numbers.
options.feedback: The word 'data' is used for both numbers and observations.

options.text: proof is impossible in any field of research.
options.feedback: Proof is possible in some fields, and the difference between the verbs is empirical.

questions.explanation:
The choice between verbs encodes the strength of the claim. Observational data support a conclusion without excluding alternatives.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A researcher writes that a result 'may be explained by'. This wording most probably indicates:
questions.context: A results section offers a candidate explanation for an unexpected pattern in the data.

options.text: a cause that the author has already proved.
options.feedback: A proved cause would be stated without a modal of possibility.

options.text: a definition of the main term of the study.
options.feedback: The phrase does not define a term; it offers an explanation.

options.text: a possible cause that has not been demonstrated.
options.feedback: Correct! 'May be' presents a candidate explanation that the study suggests without demonstrating it.

options.text: a criticism of a previous author's method.
options.feedback: No criticism of a previous author appears in the sentence.

questions.explanation:
Hedged verbs mark the certainty of a claim. 'May be' presents a candidate that the evidence allows but does not establish.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which feature most clearly identifies a paragraph as part of an academic argument rather than a news report?
questions.context: A student compares the style of a scholarly article with that of a daily newspaper report.

options.text: It reports the most recent event of the day.
options.feedback: Reporting the event of the day is a feature of news writing.

options.text: It uses short sentences and vivid adjectives.
options.feedback: Short sentences and vivid adjectives belong to journalistic narrative.

options.text: It begins with a question addressed to the reader.
options.feedback: Direct questions to the reader are characteristic of journalism, not of a scholarly argument.

options.text: It qualifies its claims with hedges such as 'may' or 'appears to'.
options.feedback: Correct! Hedging is a hallmark of academic writing because it shows how far the evidence supports a claim.

questions.explanation:
Academic authors calibrate the strength of their claims. News writing aims at direct statements, and academic prose marks uncertainty explicitly.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In a research article, the term 'prior literature' refers to:
questions.context: A reader meets the expression 'prior literature' in the introduction of a study.

options.text: the studies published earlier on the same question.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Prior literature' means the research already carried out on the same problem.

options.text: the introductory paragraphs of the same article.
options.feedback: It refers to other studies, not to the paragraphs of this article.

options.text: the personal opinions of the research team.
options.feedback: It denotes published research rather than the opinions of the team.

options.text: the bibliography compiled by a newspaper.
options.feedback: The bibliography of a newspaper is not what the term denotes.

questions.explanation:
Technical vocabulary in a paper has a fixed scope. 'Prior' means what exists before the present study, that is, previous research.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence best states a research question?
questions.context: A reader identifies the sentence in an article that states what the study sets out to find out.

options.text: The study took place in six schools during 2019.
options.feedback: The first sentence reports the setting, not the question.

options.text: To what extent does attendance affect performance in this subject?
options.feedback: Correct! The interrogative sentence that names two variables states what the study investigates.

options.text: Attendance rose in three of the six schools studied.
options.feedback: The third sentence states a result.

options.text: The data were collected through a short questionnaire.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence describes the method of collection.

questions.explanation:
A research question asks about a relationship and is expressed in interrogative form. The other sentences report design, finding and procedure.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A conclusion in an academic article typically:
questions.context: A student describes what the closing section of a research article is expected to do.

options.text: lists every source consulted in alphabetical order.
options.feedback: The list of sources belongs to the references.

options.text: describes the instruments used in the fieldwork.
options.feedback: The instruments are described in the method.

options.text: answers the research question and notes the limits of the study.
options.feedback: Correct! A conclusion answers the question that was posed and acknowledges the boundaries of the answer.

options.text: repeats the abstract word for word.
options.feedback: A conclusion interprets the findings rather than repeating the summary.

questions.explanation:
A conclusion returns to the question and qualifies the answer. It neither lists sources nor repeats the abstract literally.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The expression 'the sample was randomly assigned' is important because it:
questions.context: A reader notes a detail in the method section of an experiment about how the participants were distributed.

options.text: guarantees that the results will be true.
options.feedback: No method guarantees a true result, so 'guarantees' overstates it.

options.text: shows that every member of the population took part.
options.feedback: A sample is always smaller than the population.

options.text: means the study was repeated in several regions.
options.feedback: Randomisation concerns assignment, not the repetition of the study.

options.text: reduces the risk of systematic differences between groups.
options.feedback: Correct! Random assignment makes the groups comparable and reduces systematic bias between them.

questions.explanation:
Randomisation is a design feature. It balances known and unknown characteristics between groups, which is what its mention signals.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which of the following is a limitation rather than a justification in a research article?
questions.context: A reader distinguishes the parts of a methods section that strengthen the study from those that restrict it.

options.text: The study used a small convenience sample.
options.feedback: Correct! A small convenience sample restricts how far the results can be generalised, so it is a limitation.

options.text: The instrument was validated by two experts.
options.feedback: Validation by experts strengthens the credibility of the instrument.

options.text: The data were collected over eight months.
options.feedback: The length of the data collection period is a description of the design.

options.text: The study replicated an earlier design.
options.feedback: Replication is a strength, not a restriction.

questions.explanation:
A limitation restricts the reach of the conclusions. A small convenience sample is exactly that kind of restriction.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When an author writes 'arguably', the most probable effect on the reader is to:
questions.context: A student notes an adverb used by an author before a statement of position in an article.

options.text: state the claim as a proven fact.
options.feedback: A proven fact is stated without a hedge of this kind.

options.text: signal that the claim is reasonable but open to dispute.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Arguably' presents a defensible claim while leaving room for disagreement.

options.text: reject the claim entirely.
options.feedback: Rejecting a claim requires a different verb, such as 'contradicts' or 'refutes'.

options.text: introduce a new term that must be defined.
options.feedback: The adverb modifies the strength of a claim and introduces no new term.

questions.explanation:
Hedges and intensifiers calibrate an argument. 'Arguably' presents a claim the author believes defensible while acknowledging that others may differ.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which element of a research article states the exact number of people who took part?
questions.context: A reader looks for the exact size of the participant group described in an article.

options.text: the conclusion
options.feedback: A conclusion interprets the results and does not list the sample.

options.text: the abstract's title line
options.feedback: A title line states the subject, not the size of the sample.

options.text: the method section
options.feedback: Correct! The method section describes the participants and therefore gives their number.

options.text: the reference list
options.feedback: The reference list contains sources, not participants.

questions.explanation:
Details about the sample belong to the description of the method, which is where the reader looks for the design.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A reader who wants to know whether the findings apply to other populations should look at the:
questions.context: A practitioner considers whether the conclusions of a study can be applied to a different group of people.

options.text: title of the article
options.feedback: A title states the subject, not the reach of the findings.

options.text: number of the footnotes
options.feedback: The number of footnotes says nothing about the sample.

options.text: title of the journal
options.feedback: The name of the journal does not indicate the limits of the sample.

options.text: discussion and limitations sections
options.feedback: Correct! The limits of generalisation are set out in the discussion and the limitations.

questions.explanation:
External validity is discussed where the author states the limits of the sample. That is the discussion and the limitations.
---
questions.subject: ingles
